source: It is noon; and Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusting his pale loaf-of-bread face from the cabin-scuttle, announces dinner to his lord and master; who, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking an observation of the sun; and is now mutely reckoning the latitude on the smooth, medallion-shaped tablet, reserved for that daily purpose on the upper part of his ivory leg. From his complete inattention to the tidings, you would think that moody Ahab had not heard his menial. But presently, catching hold of the mizen shrouds, he swings himself to the deck, and in an even, unexhilarated voice, saying, “Dinner, Mr. Starbuck,” disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan’s step has died away, and Starbuck, the first Emir, has every reason to suppose that he is seated, then Starbuck rouses from his quietude, takes a few turns along the planks, and, after a grave peep into the binnacle, says, with some touch of pleasantness, “Dinner, Mr. Stubb,” and descends the scuttle. The second Emir lounges about the rigging awhile, and then slightly shaking the main brace, to see whether it will be all right with that important rope, he likewise takes up the old burden, and with a rapid “Dinner, Mr. Flask,” follows after his predecessors.

But the third Emir, now seeing himself all alone on the quarter-deck, seems to feel relieved from some curious restraint; for, tipping all sorts of knowing winks in all sorts of directions, and kicking off his shoes, he strikes into a sharp but noiseless squall of a hornpipe right over the Grand Turk’s head; and then, by a dexterous sleight, pitching his cap up into the mizentop for a shelf, he goes down rollicking so far at least as he remains visible from the deck, reversing all other processions, by bringing up the rear with music. But ere stepping into the cabin doorway below, he pauses, ships a new face altogether, and, then, independent, hilarious little Flask enters King Ahab’s presence, in the character of Abjectus, or the Slave.

It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificialness of sea-usages, that while in the open air of the deck some officers will, upon provocation, bear themselves boldly and defyingly enough towards their commander; yet, ten to one, let those very officers the next moment go down to their customary dinner in that same commander’s cabin, and straightway their inoffensive, not to say deprecatory and humble air towards him, as he sits at the head of the table; this is marvellous, sometimes most comical. Wherefore this difference? A problem? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon; and to have been Belshazzar, not haughtily but courteously, therein certainly must have been some touch of mundane grandeur. But he who in the rightly regal and intelligent spirit presides over his own private dinner-table of invited guests, that man’s unchallenged power and dominion of individual influence for the time; that man’s royalty of state transcends Belshazzar’s, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Who has but once dined his friends, has tasted what it is to be Cæsar. It is a witchery of social czarship which there is no withstanding. Now, if to this consideration you superadd the official supremacy of a ship-master, then, by inference, you will derive the cause of that peculiarity of sea-life just mentioned.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. In his own proper turn, each officer waited to be served. They were as little children before Ahab; and yet, in Ahab, there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened upon the old man’s knife, as he carved the chief dish before him. I do not suppose that for the world they would have profaned that moment with the slightest observation, even upon so neutral a topic as the weather. No! And when reaching out his knife and fork, between which the slice of beef was locked, Ahab thereby motioned Starbuck’s plate towards him, the mate received his meat as though receiving alms; and cut it tenderly; and a little started if, perchance, the knife grazed against the plate; and chewed it noiselessly; and swallowed it, not without circumspection. For, like the Coronation banquet at Frankfort, where the German Emperor profoundly dines with the seven Imperial Electors, so these cabin meals were somehow solemn meals, eaten in awful silence; and yet at table old Ahab forbade not conversation; only he himself was dumb. What a relief it was to choking Stubb, when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below. And poor little Flask, he was the youngest son, and little boy of this weary family party. His were the shinbones of the saline beef; his would have been the drumsticks. For Flask to have presumed to help himself, this must have seemed to him tantamount to larceny in the first degree. Had he helped himself at that table, doubtless, never more would he have been able to hold his head up in this honest world; nevertheless, strange to say, Ahab never forbade him. And had Flask helped himself, the chances were Ahab had never so much as noticed it. Least of all, did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the owners of the ship denied it to him, on account of its clotting his clear, sunny complexion; or whether he deemed that, on so long a voyage in such marketless waters, butter was at a premium, and therefore was not for him, a subaltern; however it was, Flask, alas! was a butterless man!

Another thing. Flask was the last person down at the dinner, and Flask is the first man up. Consider! For hereby Flask’s dinner was badly jammed in point of time. Starbuck and Stubb both had the start of him; and yet they also have the privilege of lounging in the rear. If Stubb even, who is but a peg higher than Flask, happens to have but a small appetite, and soon shows symptoms of concluding his repast, then Flask must bestir himself, he will not get more than three mouthfuls that day; for it is against holy usage for Stubb to precede Flask to the deck. Therefore it was that Flask once admitted in private, that ever since he had arisen to the dignity of an officer, from that moment he had never known what it was to be otherwise than hungry, more or less. For what he ate did not so much relieve his hunger, as keep it immortal in him. Peace and satisfaction, thought Flask, have for ever departed from my stomach. I am an officer; but, how I wish I could fish a bit of old-fashioned beef in the forecastle, as I used to when I was before the mast. There’s the fruits of promotion now; there’s the vanity of glory: there’s the insanity of life! Besides, if it were so that any mere sailor of the Pequod had a grudge against Flask in Flask’s official capacity, all that sailor had to do, in order to obtain ample vengeance, was to go aft at dinner-time, and get a peep at Flask through the cabin sky-light, sitting silly and dumfoundered before awful Ahab.

Now, Ahab and his three mates formed what may be called the first table in the Pequod’s cabin. After their departure, taking place in inverted order to their arrival, the canvas cloth was cleared, or rather was restored to some hurried order by the pallid steward. And then the three harpooneers were bidden to the feast, they being its residuary legatees. They made a sort of temporary servants’ hall of the high and mighty cabin.

In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint and nameless invisible domineerings of the captain’s table, was the entire care-free license and ease, the almost frantic democracy of those inferior fellows the harpooneers. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of the hinges of their own jaws, the harpooneers chewed their food with such a relish that there was a report to it. They dined like lords; they filled their bellies like Indian ships all day loading with spices. Such portentous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego, that to fill out the vacancies made by the previous repast, often the pale Dough-Boy was fain to bring on a great baron of salt-junk, seemingly quarried out of the solid ox. And if he were not lively about it, if he did not go with a nimble hop-skip-and-jump, then Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of accelerating him by darting a fork at his back, harpoon-wise. And once Daggoo, seized with a sudden humor, assisted Dough-Boy’s memory by snatching him up bodily, and thrusting his head into a great empty wooden trencher, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began laying out the circle preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, shuddering sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward; the progeny of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the standing spectacle of the black terrific Ahab, and the periodical tumultuous visitations of these three savages, Dough-Boy’s whole life was one continual lip-quiver. Commonly, after seeing the harpooneers furnished with all things they demanded, he would escape from their clutches into his little pantry adjoining, and fearfully peep out at them through the blinds of its door, till all was over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated over against Tashtego, opposing his filed teeth to the Indian’s: crosswise to them, Daggoo seated on the floor, for a bench would have brought his hearse-plumed head to the low carlines; at every motion of his colossal limbs, making the low cabin framework to shake, as when an African elephant goes passenger in a ship. But for all this, the great negro was wonderfully abstemious, not to say dainty. It seemed hardly possible that by such comparatively small mouthfuls he could keep up the vitality diffused through so broad, baronial, and superb a person. But, doubtless, this noble savage fed strong and drank deep of the abounding element of air; and through his dilated nostrils snuffed in the sublime life of the worlds. Not by beef or by bread, are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg, he had a mortal, barbaric smack of the lip in eating—an ugly sound enough—so much so, that the trembling Dough-Boy almost looked to see whether any marks of teeth lurked in his own lean arms. And when he would hear Tashtego singing out for him to produce himself, that his bones might be picked, the simple-witted steward all but shattered the crockery hanging round him in the pantry, by his sudden fits of the palsy. Nor did the whetstone which the harpooneers carried in their pockets, for their lances and other weapons; and with which whetstones, at dinner, they would ostentatiously sharpen their knives; that grating sound did not at all tend to tranquillize poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his Island days, Queequeg, for one, must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, convivial indiscretions. Alas! Dough-Boy! hard fares the white waiter who waits upon cannibals. Not a napkin should he carry on his arm, but a buckler. In good time, though, to his great delight, the three salt-sea warriors would rise and depart; to his credulous, fable-mongering ears, all their martial bones jingling in them at every step, like Moorish scimetars in scabbards.

But, though these barbarians dined in the cabin, and nominally lived there; still, being anything but sedentary in their habits, they were scarcely ever in it except at mealtimes, and just before sleeping-time, when they passed through it to their own peculiar quarters.

In this one matter, Ahab seemed no exception to most American whale captains, who, as a set, rather incline to the opinion that by rights the ship’s cabin belongs to them; and that it is by courtesy alone that anybody else is, at any time, permitted there. So that, in real truth, the mates and harpooneers of the Pequod might more properly be said to have lived out of the cabin than in it. For when they did enter it, it was something as a street-door enters a house; turning inwards for a moment, only to be turned out the next; and, as a permanent thing, residing in the open air. Nor did they lose much hereby; in the cabin was no companionship; socially, Ahab was inaccessible. Though nominally included in the census of Christendom, he was still an alien to it. He lived in the world, as the last of the Grisly Bears lived in settled Missouri. Then the three harpooners were invited to the feast, being its residuary legatees — the heirs to whatever was left. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the high and mighty cabin.

In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint and nameless invisible domineering of the captain's table was the entire carefree license and ease, the almost frantic democracy, of those inferior fellows the harpooners. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of the hinges of their own jaws, the harpooners chewed their food with such relish that there was a report to it. They dined like lords; they filled their bellies like Indian ships loading with spices all day. Such portentous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego that, to fill the gaps left by the previous meal, the pale Dough-Boy often had to bring on a great baron of salt-junk (salt beef), seemingly quarried out of the solid ox. And if he was not lively about it, if he did not go with a nimble hop-skip-and-jump, then Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of speeding him up by darting a fork at his back, harpoon-fashion. And once Daggoo, seized with a sudden humor, assisted Dough-Boy's memory by snatching him up bodily and thrusting his head into a great empty wooden trencher, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began laying out the circle preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, shuddering sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward, the offspring of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the standing spectacle of the black, terrifying Ahab and the periodic tumultuous visitations of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continual lip-quiver. Usually, after seeing the harpooners furnished with everything they demanded, he would escape from their clutches into his little pantry next door, and fearfully peep out at them through the blinds of its door until it was all over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated opposite Tashtego, pitting his filed teeth against the Indian's; crosswise to them, Daggoo sat on the floor, for a bench would have brought his hearse-plumed head up against the low carlines (the beams under the deck overhead); at every motion of his colossal limbs he made the low cabin framework shake, as when an African elephant travels as a passenger in a ship. But for all this, the great negro was wonderfully abstemious, not to say dainty. It seemed hardly possible that by such comparatively small mouthfuls he could keep up the vitality spread through so broad, baronial, and superb a person. But doubtless this noble savage fed strong and drank deep of the abounding element of air, and through his dilated nostrils snuffed in the sublime life of the worlds. Not by beef or by bread are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg — he had a mortal, barbaric smack of the lip in eating, an ugly enough sound, so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost looked to see whether any teeth marks lurked in his own lean arms. And when he heard Tashtego singing out for him to show himself, so that his bones might be picked, the simple-witted steward all but shattered the crockery hanging around him in the pantry with his sudden fits of the palsy. Nor did the whetstones the harpooners carried in their pockets for their lances and other weapons — whetstones on which, at dinner, they would ostentatiously sharpen their knives — nor did that grating sound at all tend to calm poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his Island days, Queequeg, for one, must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, convivial indiscretions? Alas, Dough-Boy! Hard fares the white waiter who waits on cannibals. Not a napkin should he carry on his arm, but a buckler. In good time, though, to his great delight, the three salt-sea warriors would rise and depart — to his credulous, fable-mongering ears, all their martial bones jingling in them at every step, like Moorish scimitars in scabbards.

But although these barbarians ate in the cabin and in name lived there, their habits were anything but sedentary, and so they were almost never in it except at mealtimes and just before bed, when they passed through on their way to their own particular quarters.

On this one point Ahab seemed no different from most American whaling captains, who, as a class, tend to think the ship's cabin belongs to them by right, and that anyone else is allowed in it only as a courtesy. So, in plain truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more accurately be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. For when they did go in, it was rather the way a street door goes into a house: it swings inward for a moment, only to be swung back out the next, and it lives, permanently, in the open air. Not that they lost much by this; there was no companionship in the cabin; socially, Ahab was unapproachable. Though he was nominally counted in the census of Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world the way the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as, when spring and summer had gone, that wild Logan of the woods would bury himself in a hollow tree and live out the winter there, sucking his own paws, so in his harsh, howling old age Ahab's soul, shut up in the hollowed trunk of his body, fed there on the sullen paws of its gloom!

modern_da.title: Kapitel 34 — Kahytsbordet
paragraphs: Det er middag, og Dough-Boy, stewarden, stikker sit blege ansigt, der ligner brøddej, op fra kahytsluget for at melde, at maden er klar, til sin herre og hersker. Ahab sidder i den læsidede hvalbåd agter. Han har lige taget solhøjden og regner nu tavst breddegraden ud på den glatte, medaljonformede tavle, der er forbeholdt dette daglige formål øverst på hans elfenbensben. Når man ser, hvor fuldstændig han ignorerer beskeden, skulle man tro, at den tungsindige Ahab ikke havde hørt sin tjener. Men lidt efter griber han fat i mesanvanterne, svinger sig ned på dækket og siger med jævn, ligegyldig stemme: »Middag, Mr. Starbuck,« og forsvinder ind i kahytten.

Da det sidste ekko af sultanens skridt er forsvundet, og Starbuck, den første emir, har al mulig grund til at tro, at sultanen er kommet til bords, vågner Starbuck af sin ro, går nogle ture frem og tilbage på dækket og kigger alvorligt ind i binnaklen (kompashuset). Så siger han med et strejf af venlighed: »Middag, Mr. Stubb,« og går ned. Den anden emir driver en stund rundt i rigningen og rusker så lidt i storbrassen for at se, om alt er i orden med det vigtige tov. Han tager også det gamle omkvæd op og følger med et hurtigt »Middag, Mr. Flask« efter sine forgængere.

Men den tredje emir, der nu finder sig helt alene på agterdækket, ser ud til at føle sig befriet for en eller anden mærkelig tvang. For han sender alle mulige vidende blink til alle sider, sparker skoene af og går i gang med en hurtig, men lydløs byge af en hornpipe lige over Den Store Tyrks hoved. Så kaster han behændigt sin kasket op i mesantoppen, så den kan ligge der som på en hylde, og går rullende og lystigt ned — i det mindste så længe man kan se ham fra dækket — og vender alle andre optog på hovedet ved at gå sidst med musikken. Men før han træder gennem kahytsdøren dernede, standser han, sætter et helt nyt ansigt på, og så træder den selvstændige, muntre lille Flask ind til kong Ahab i rollen som Abjectus, Slaven.

Det er ikke det mindste blandt de underlige ting, som havets overdrevne kunstighed avler, at nogle officerer, når de bliver provokeret, på det åbne dæk kan optræde dristigt og trodsigt nok over for deres kommandør. Alligevel kan man slå fast, ti mod en, at lader man de samme officerer gå ned i næste øjeblik til deres sædvanlige middag i den samme kommandørs kahyt, så er deres uskyldige, for ikke at sige undskyldende og ydmyge væsen over for ham, mens han sidder for bordenden, forbløffende og somme tider yderst komisk. Hvorfor denne forskel? Et problem? Måske ikke. At have været Belsazar, Babylons konge, og at have været Belsazar ikke hovmodigt, men høfligt — heri må der bestemt have været noget af verdslig storhed. Men den mand, der på rigtig kongelig og klog vis præsiderer ved sit eget private middagsbord blandt indbudte gæster — hans uanfægtede magt og personlige indflydelse i det øjeblik, hans kongelige værdighed, overgår Belsazars, for Belsazar var ikke den største. Enhver, der bare én gang har haft sine venner til middag, har smagt, hvad det er at være Cæsar. Det er en trolddom af socialt zarvælde, som ingen kan modstå. Lægger man nu oven i det en skibskaptajns officielle overherredømme, så når man frem til årsagen til den ejendommelighed ved livet til søs, som netop er nævnt.

Ved sit elfenbensindlagte bord præsiderede Ahab som en stum, manet havløve på den hvide koralstrand, omgivet af sine krigeriske, men stadig ærbødige unger. Hver officer ventede på at blive serveret i sin rette tur. De var som små børn over for Ahab, og alligevel syntes der ikke at ligge den mindste sociale hovmodighed i Ahab. Som ét sind havde de alle fæstnet de spændte øjne på den gamle mands kniv, mens han skar for sig af hovedretten. Jeg tror ikke, de for noget i verden ville have vanhelliget det øjeblik med den mindste bemærkning, selv om emnet var så neutralt som vejret. Nej! Og da Ahab rakte kniv og gaffel frem med oksestykket spændt fast imellem dem og dermed vinkede Starbucks tallerken hen til sig, tog styrmanden imod sit kød, som modtog han en almisse, og skar det blidt og for sammen i et lille sæt, hvis kniven skrabede mod tallerkenen, og tyggede det lydløst og slugte det, ikke uden forsigtighed. For ligesom kroningsfesten i Frankfurt, hvor den tyske kejser spiser i dyb højtidelighed sammen med de syv kurfyrster, var disse måltider i kahytten på en eller anden måde højtidelige måltider, spist i ærefrygtindgydende tavshed. Og alligevel forbød gamle Ahab ikke at tale ved bordet; det var bare ham selv, der var tavs. Hvilken lettelse var det ikke for den halvkvalte Stubb, når en rotte pludselig larmede nede i lasten. Og stakkels lille Flask — han var den yngste søn og den lille dreng i dette trætte familieselskab. Hans var skinnebenene af det saltede oksekød; hans ville trommestikkerne have været. For Flask at tillade sig selv at tage for sig må have føltes som groft tyveri. Havde han forsynet sig ved det bord, ville han uden tvivl aldrig mere have kunnet løfte hovedet i denne ærlige verden; men besynderligt nok forbød Ahab ham det aldrig. Og havde Flask forsynet sig, var der god chance for, at Ahab slet ikke ville have lagt mærke til det. Allermindst tillod Flask sig at tage smør. Om han troede, at skibets ejere nægtede ham det, fordi det ville klumpe hans klare, solrige hudfarve, eller om han regnede med, at smør på så lang en rejse i så markedsløse farvande var en kostbarhed og derfor ikke noget for ham, en underordnet — hvordan det end var, så var Flask, ak, en mand uden smør!

Endnu noget: Flask var den sidste, der kom ned til middag, og den første, der gik op igen. Tænk over det! Det betød, at Flasks middag var slemt knebet på tid. Starbuck og Stubb havde begge et forspring på ham, men de havde også ret til at blive siddende. Hvis selv Stubb, der kun står ét trin over Flask, tilfældigvis havde ringe appetit og viste tegn på at være færdig med sit måltid, så måtte Flask skynde sig — så fik han ikke mere end tre mundfulde den dag, for det stred mod den hellige skik, at Stubb forlod bordet før Flask. Derfor betroede Flask engang i al fortrolighed, at lige siden han var steget til officersværdighed, havde han aldrig kendt til andet end at være sulten, mere eller mindre. Det, han spiste, stillede ikke så meget hans sult som holdt den i live for evigt. Fred og tilfredshed, mente Flask, er for altid veget fra min mave. Jeg er officer — men hvor ville jeg ønske, jeg kunne snuppe et stykke godt gammeldags oksekød i mandskabsrummet, som jeg plejede som menig matros. Der har man frugten af forfremmelse. Der har man herlighedens forfængelighed. Der har man livets vanvid! Og desuden: Hvis en almindelig matros på Pequod nærede nag til Flask i hans officielle egenskab, behøvede han kun gå agterud ved middagstid og kigge på Flask gennem kahytsoverlyset, hvor han sad dér, fjoget og målløs foran den frygtelige Ahab, så fik han rigelig hævn.

Nu udgjorde Ahab og hans tre styrmænd det, man kunne kalde det første bord i Pequods kahyt. Efter deres afgang, i omvendt rækkefølge af deres ankomst, blev lærredsdugen ryddet — eller rettere bragt i en eller anden hastig orden af den blege steward. Så blev de tre harpunerer indbudt til festen, som dens resterende arvinger — arvingerne til alt, hvad der var levnet. De gjorde den høje og mægtige kahyt til en slags midlertidig tjenerhal.

I mærkværdig kontrast til den næsten uudholdelige tvang og navnløse usynlige herskesyge ved kaptajnens bord stod den fuldstændig ubekymrede frihed og lethed, det næsten rasende demokrati, hos de underordnede fyre, harpunerne. Mens deres herrer, styrmændene, virkede bange for lyden af hængslerne i deres egne kæber, tyggede harpunererne deres mad med sådan en velsmag, at det knaldede. De spiste som lorder; de fyldte deres maver som indiske skibe, der læsser krydderier hele dagen. Queequeg og Tashtego havde så uhyrlige appetitter, at den blege Dough-Boy ofte måtte slæbe et stort lændestykke af saltet oksekød (salt-junk) ind, som om det var brudt ud af selve oksen, for at fylde hullerne efter det forrige måltid. Og hvis han ikke var rap til det, hvis han ikke gik i en adræt hoppende gang, så havde Tashtego en ugentlemanagtig måde at sætte fart i ham på ved at slynge en gaffel mod hans ryg, ligesom en harpun. Og engang hjalp Daggoo, grebet af et pludseligt indfald, Dough-Boys hukommelse på vej ved at snuppe ham op i hele hans person og stikke hans hoved ned i et stort tomt træfad, mens Tashtego med kniven i hånden begyndte at tegne cirklen som forberedelse til at skalpere ham. Han var af natur en meget nervøs, skælvende lille fyr, denne steward med brødansigtet, afkom af en bankerot bager og en hospitalssygeplejerske. Og med det stående syn af den sorte, skræmmende Ahab og de tre vildes jævnlige larmende besøg var hele Dough-Boys liv ét uafbrudt læbeskælv. Som regel, når han havde set til, at harpunererne fik alt, hvad de forlangte, slap han ud af deres kløer ind i sit lille spisekammer ved siden af og kiggede frygtsomt ud på dem gennem persiennerne i dets dør, indtil det hele var overstået.

Det var et syn at se Queequeg sidde over for Tashtego og sætte sine filede tænder op mod indianerens. På tværs af dem sad Daggoo på gulvet, for en bænk ville have bragt hans hoved, der bar fjerbusk som en ligvogn, op mod de lave dæksbjælker (bjælkerne under dækket ovenover). For hver bevægelse af hans kolossale lemmer rystede kahyttens lave tømmerværk, som når en afrikansk elefant rejser som passager på et skib. Men trods alt dette var den store sorte mand forbavsende nøjsom, for ikke at sige kræsen. Det virkede næsten umuligt, at han med så forholdsvis små mundfulde kunne holde livskraften oppe i en så bred, fyrstelig og pragtfuld skikkelse. Men denne ædle vilde var uden tvivl mæt af luft og drak dybt af det rigelige element, og gennem sine opspilede næsebor indåndede han verdenernes ophøjede liv. Ikke af oksekød eller brød skabes og næres kæmper. Men Queequeg — han smaskede dødeligt og barbarisk med læben, når han spiste, en grim nok lyd, så meget, at den skælvende Dough-Boy nærmest kiggede efter, om der var spor af tandmærker på hans egne magre arme. Og da han hørte Tashtego råbe, at han skulle vise sig, så hans knogler kunne blive gnavet rene, var den enfoldige stuert lige ved at slå porcelænet, der hang rundt om ham i spisekammeret, i stykker med sine pludselige rystelsesanfald. Heller ikke de hvæssesten, som harpunererne bar i lommerne til lanser og andre våben — sten, som de ved middagen demonstrativt hvæssede deres knive på — heller ikke den skurrende lyd var på nogen måde egnet til at berolige stakkels Dough-Boy. Hvordan kunne han glemme, at Queequeg i hvert fald i sine dage på øen sikkert havde gjort sig skyldig i nogle morderiske, selskabelige udskejelser? Ak, Dough-Boy! Hårdt er det for en hvid tjener at vente op for kannibaler. Han skulle ikke have en serviet over armen, men et skjold. Men omsider plejede de tre saltvandskrigere, til hans store glæde, at rejse sig og gå — og for hans godtroende, sagnlystne ører klirrede alle deres krigerknogler i dem ved hvert skridt, som maurernes sabler i skederne.

Men selv om disse barbarer spiste i kahytten og på papiret boede der, var deres vaner alt andet end stillesiddende, og derfor var de næsten aldrig i den undtagen ved måltiderne og lige før sengetid, når de gik igennem på vej til deres egne særlige kvarterer.

På dette ene punkt adskilte Ahab sig ikke fra de fleste amerikanske hvalfangerkaptajner, der som klasse har tendens til at mene, at skibets kahyt tilhører dem med rette, og at alle andre kun har lov at komme ind i den som en venlighed. Så i al ærlighed kunne man med større ret sige, at Pequods styrmænd og harpunerer boede uden for kahytten end i den. For når de gik ind, var det snarere, som en gadedør går ind i et hus: Den svinger indad et øjeblik, kun for i det næste at svinge ud igen, og den bor for stedse under åben himmel. Ikke at de tabte meget derved; der var intet selskab i kahytten; socialt var Ahab uopnåelig. Selv om han nominelt var talt med i kristenhedens folketælling, var han stadig en fremmed for den. Han levede i verden, som den sidste grizzlybjørn levede i det bosatte Missouri. Og ligesom den vilde Logan fra skovene, når forår og sommer var forbi, begravede sig i et hult træ og tilbragte vinteren der med at suge på sine egne poter, sådan fodrede Ahabs sjæl, indesluttet i hans krops udhulede stamme, sig i hans barske, hylende alderdom på sin dystre mismods sure poter!
